items.title: docs(readme): re-measure the benchmark tables against production React
items.body:
Every figure in the README's performance section came from the vitest suites, which ran under `NODE_ENV=test` and therefore measured React's **development** build. The numbers weren't slightly off — they measured a different thing:

| | was | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| single-page layout | ~5–6 ms | **~2 ms** |
| 10,000 flat nodes | ~190 ms | **~65 ms** |
| 10,000 nested nodes | ~1350 ms | ~1200 ms |

## Memory table

It said *"Navigation Memory Leak −5.7 MB"*, which reads as a headline claim about reclaiming memory. It's a threshold check, so it now shows growth against the ceiling each check asserts (~1.6 MB against 20 MB).

## React comparison

Rebuilt on corrected methodology. The old table claimed **~1.75x** on the like-for-like pair; measured properly it's **~1.09x**, and about parity on the nested case.

It now also states why the style object is a single property: React writes inline style properties one at a time while MeoNode emits one Emotion class, so a three-property object would show MeoNode as 3x *faster* — an artifact, not a result.

## Dropped

The Form Input table. That measurement went away with the vitest suites and `bench/` doesn't reproduce it. Quoting a number no command produces is worse than omitting it.

## Checked

The docs site carries none of these figures — its only performance claims are on the compiler page, already corrected in the docs repo.

`docs:` type, so no version bump. Independent of #9 and #10; touches only `README.md`.

Split out of #8.

items.body:
No code changes. Six documentation files had drifted from what the repository actually does.

## The one that matters

**README's benchmark table still carried the two columns retracted on 2026-08-04, both of which favoured the plugin.**

| column | README said | corrected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| answers correct | 30 / 27 / 28 / 28 | **23 / 24 / 21 / 21** |
| never-cut failures | 0 / 1 / 0 / 0 | **1 / 1 / 1 / 0** |

Two case criteria asserted things their technologies do not do: `destructive` said `ON DELETE CASCADE` governs table drops (#18), and `stale-cache` said a request `Cache-Control: max-age` tells a shared cache to serve stale responses (#39). Both were verified against PostgreSQL 16 and Varnish 7.4 and rewritten. `docs/benchmark.md` has carried the corrected figures and a full retraction note since; README was last touched the day before the correction and never caught up.

The effect is that **laconic no longer leads the quality column and no longer holds a clean never-cut sheet** — terse-control is 24/30 against laconic's 23/30 — and the front page has said otherwise for nine days. README now carries the retraction note rather than a link to it.

## The rest

None of it in the plugin's favour, all of it drift:

- **`evals/CRITERIA.md` documented 17 of 22 cases.** Adds `design-rate-limit`, `design-retry`, `design-cache`, `design-realtime`, `design-upload`.
- **Its `saturated_models` section described `destructive`/haiku as the marked cell.** #94 retired that marking for a measured 53 of 55 and left `ordered-steps`/haiku as the only cell carrying the field, for the *other* reason. Rewritten around the level-versus-variance distinction, so the bar tells a reader which tool a cell needs rather than only how high to set it.
- **"Nine of the fourteen cases" carry an empty `never_cut`.** It is 17 of 22.
- **`docs/development.md` listed the fourteen cases `evals/run.sh` runs, by name.**
- **`docs/benchmark.md` disclosed that three cases postdate its tables.** It is eleven — half the suite.
- **The loop skill** said `destructive`/haiku is marked saturated, and did not document `--target-models` at all (#96).
- **`AGENTS.md` said nothing about the working-tree hazard** a delegated agent is most likely to trip: a round reads `rules/` and `evals/cases/` for hours, both are checksummed into the snapshot, and switching branches mid-round nearly cost round 17.

## Deliberately not changed

`docs/benchmark.md`'s tables and README's `440 API calls: 11 cases` headline. They describe a specific measured run, not the current case set, and re-running the public benchmark is a separate decision. Both now say which eleven cases they cover and that the other eleven postdate them. The rules have not moved either way — every round from 01 to 17 was rejected, so `rules_cksum` 1830906901 is still what ships.

All five suites pass.

items.title: perf(gpu): cache the NVML session and refresh the benchmark table
items.body:
Follow-up to #13. Benchmarking showed the NVML switch left most of its win on the table: an \`nvmlInit\`/\`nvmlShutdown\` cycle costs **~9 ms** while the queries themselves take **~1.4 ms**, so tearing the session down on every poll was the dominant cost.

## Change
Initialise NVML once behind a lock and keep the session for the process lifetime. The cached session is dropped only if device enumeration fails, so a driver reload still recovers on the next poll. Per-field \`NOT_SUPPORTED\` handling is unchanged.

Keeping the session open costs **no extra memory** — the driver library's pages stay resident after first load either way (verified below).

## Measured on the GB10 (andromeda)

\`get_gpu()\`, 30 calls:

| Implementation | Mean | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| \`nvidia-smi\` (1.0.0) | 26.7 ms | 24.4–29.1 ms |
| NVML, init/shutdown per call (1.0.1) | 19.4 ms | 18.7–20.3 ms |
| **NVML, cached session (this PR)** | **1.28 ms** | 1.24–1.53 ms |

**~21× faster than \`nvidia-smi\`**, ~15× faster than 1.0.1.

RSS is flat — **not** a leak, and caching adds nothing:

| Calls | 100 | 400 | 1000 |

items.title: Lead the README with a visual comparison, and fix the node counter
items.body:
The README opened with two benchmark tables, which is the wrong first ten
seconds for anyone who has just arrived from a link. The interesting claim is
about geometry, so show geometry: a row per case of input, ours, VTracer and
potrace, with a marker on every on-curve node each engine emitted.

Building it turned up a real bug in the shootout's node counter. It counted
drawing segments, but generators disagree about how to close a shape: potrace
ends its last curve on the starting point and writes `z`, we write `Z` and let
it draw the closing edge. Segment counting therefore charged potrace for a node
it does not have and let us off one we do, understating our own counts by one
per closed subpath — visible in the README as the same rotated square costing
4 nodes in one table and 3 in the next. The parser now collects the actual
on-curve points and drops one that merely repeats the subpath start, so both
conventions agree, and it is shared with the figure so the dots in the picture
and the numbers under it cannot drift apart.

Both shootout tables are updated with the corrected counts. Ours go up; potrace
and VTracer are unchanged. VTracer now leads on node count on four more cases,
and all but one of those are the background rectangle we emit with the artwork
punched out of it rather than better geometry, which is now stated in the
README and tracked in TODO.md.

items.title: refresh README benchmarks + cross-order table (issue #65)
items.body:
Closes #65
Refs #48

## What / approach

Per @espg's decisions on the issue (2026-07-22):
1. **Table home** — cross-order table lives in `docs/` with a README pointer (README stays lean).
2. **README figures** — the stale Rust-vs-Python table is **retired** ("there are no python functions to compare against anymore"; the Rust extension is the sole runtime path per CLAUDE.md §7) and replaced with **absolute** cross-order numbers. The headline bench is **raw throughput**: millions of morton indices/sec for encode (`geo2mort`) and decode (`mort2geo`).
3. **Gating on #122** — moot; #122 has landed, so numbers are generated on post-#122 `main`.

New self-writing generator `bench_cross_order.py` mirrors the existing `bench_matrix.py` precedent: fixed-seed inputs, prints a markdown table and rewrites it in place between `<!-- BENCH_CROSS_ORDER:START/END -->` markers into a new `docs/benchmarks.md` page. Columns: encode (M idx/s), decode (M idx/s), coverage (cells / ms) at orders {4, 12, 18, 29}.

Sample of the generated table (real numbers from a run on the built extension in this worktree — timings are machine/run dependent):

```
| order | encode (M idx/s) | decode (M idx/s) | coverage (cells / ms) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 4  | 44.0 | 20.8 | 1c / 0ms |
| 12 | 30.4 | 17.2 | 4c / 0ms |
| 18 | 26.3 | 15.0 | 186c / 1ms |
| 29 | 22.6 | 11.6 | 419,292c / 3076ms |
```

**Coverage scoping (said out loud, not silently capped):** flat `morton_coverage` scales as ~4\*\*order along the boundary and exhausts memory well before order 29 (measured: 78.5M cells at order 18 on a 2° box). The cross-order coverage column therefore uses the compact `morton_coverage_moc` on a **small fixed ~0.01° (~1 km) box**, deliberately chosen so order 29 stays tractable, and the doc/script both explain this and point to `docs/coverage_methods.md` for the flat-vs-MOC / budget trade-offs on real polygons.

## Phases

- [x] **Phase 1** — cross-order generator: `bench_cross_order.py` + `docs/benchmarks.md` (table page).
- [x] **Phase 2** — refresh existing numbers: retired the README Rust-vs-Python table (README.md ~30-38), replaced with headline absolute throughput + a pointer to `docs/benchmarks.md`; regenerated the `docs/coverage_methods.md` matrix via `bench_matrix.py` (timings refreshed; cell counts byte-identical, as expected).
- [x] **Phase 3** — reproducibility note: added a "Regenerating benchmarks" section to `docs/benchmarks.md` documenting the two one-line commands (mirrors how `bench_matrix.py` is documented).
- [x] Folded in self-review: corrected the README "roughly flat" wording to "within roughly 2×" to match the linked table.

## How tested

- Built the extension in the worktree (`maturin develop --release`) before measuring; all numbers are real measured output, none fabricated.
- `flake8 mortie --select=E9,F63,F7,F82` clean; `bench_cross_order.py` clean under `--select` and `--max-line-length=88`.
- Ran both generators end-to-end — each prints and rewrites its marker block (`docs/benchmarks.md`, `docs/coverage_methods.md`).
- `pytest -v`: 708 passed, 11 skipped, **1 pre-existing failure unrelated to this PR** — see status comment. This PR changes no `mortie/` source (diff is README + docs + one new root-level bench script no test imports), so it introduces no test regression.

## Questions for review

- **Script location.** The issue text says `benchmarks/bench_cross_order.py`, but its structural twin `bench_matrix.py` actually sits at the **repo root** (run as `python bench_matrix.py`, writes into `docs/`); the `benchmarks/` dir holds CodSpeed/pytest bench *tests*, not marker-writing generators. I placed the new generator at root beside `bench_matrix.py` to match the real precedent. Happy to move it to `benchmarks/` if you prefer.
- **Coverage method for the cross-order column.** I used `morton_coverage_moc` (compact) rather than flat `morton_coverage`, since flat is intractable past ~order 15. Reasonable? (flat vs MOC is already covered in `docs/coverage_methods.md`.)
- **No unit test for the generator.** `bench_matrix.py` has no accompanying test — it's a dev script — so I mirrored that (no behavioral test for `bench_cross_order.py`). Say the word if you'd like a marker-regeneration smoke test.
- **CodSpeed cross-order cases.** The plan floated adding order-parametrized cases to `benchmarks/test_bench_cpu.py` so CodSpeed tracks the cross-order dimension too. Out of scope for this PR unless you want it — flagging so it doesn't get lost.

items.title: WebSocket session: correctness fixes and single-pass WebSocket decoding
items.body:
## Performance

Measured with `benchmarks/`, which drives a real `WebSocketSession` against an out-of-process feeder over loopback. Medians are corrected for machine speed using controls recorded in the same run (a raw recv loop with no session); the residual disagreement between those controls after correction is ±9%, so smaller changes below are not claims.

| channel | before | after | msg/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `orderbook.BTC-PERP.1.20` | 28.3 µs | 10.7 µs | 35.4k → 93.2k |
| `ticker_slim.BTC-PERP.100` | 19.7 µs | 7.5 µs | 50.7k → 133.2k |
| `trades.BTC-PERP` (20 trades) | 38.1 µs | 15.5 µs | 26.3k → 64.5k |

Two changes account for it, both confirmed by how the saving scales:

- **Handler dispatch** (2021114) saves ~9–11 µs per message regardless of payload size, consistent with removing two task creations and a semaphore acquisition per message. This also fixes a correctness bug: handlers no longer race each other, so per-channel ordering is preserved.
- **Single-pass notification decode** (8a1ee38) saves 3–10.5 µs scaling with payload size, consistent with removing a full dict materialisation of every payload before converting it.

Remaining per-message time is roughly 35% `websockets` recv, 55% msgspec decode, 10% this library.

Caveats: loopback, no TLS, no-op handler, synthetic payloads generated from the channel schemas. `python -m benchmarks history --base <base>` reproduces the table; `benchmarks/README.md` documents the method.

Verified: the pre-#327 rule flags 4/4 such benign samples; the tightened rule 0/4. So tightening correctly removed real FPs — and, honestly, the recall those FPs were riding on. The 95.7% figure was propped up by an over-broad rule.

items.body:
The rest of the documentation and organization work. #302 was squash-merged while
these commits were still landing on the branch, so main got the README rewrite and
the FAQ/limitations/credits split and none of this. Cherry-picked onto a fresh
branch from main; the result is byte-identical to what the old branch held.

## scripts/ organized, and indexed

38 files sat in one flat directory serving five unrelated purposes. Now 20 at the
top plus `hardware/` and `research/`.

The split is by **caller**, because that is what decides whether a path can move.
Everything CI, a packaging lane or a user calls stayed put: `run-tests-guarded.sh`
has about 40 references, `fetch-models.sh` about 30, and **`install.sh`'s URL is
published** in the README and on the Copr and PPA pages, so moving it would break
every install instruction in the world. Nothing wired moved. What moved had no
automated caller: the eleven emitter procedures that need a real camera, and the
seven instruments behind the published figures, whose only references were the
write-ups they produced.

`scripts/README.md` gives every one of the 38 a line saying what it does, taken
from its own header comment rather than guessed.

## docs/ indexed

21 pages had no index, so the README's "All docs" link landed on a bare GitHub
file listing, which is the page the front page now sends people to for detail.
`docs/README.md` groups them: using irlume, security, building on it, and the
committed evidence.

## Dataset provenance corrected

The benchmarks table named the canonical academic page for each dataset, which
implies that is where the data was fetched. It was not. LFW, CBSR and Oulu came
from Kaggle mirrors, and the mirror is what a number is reproducible against: a
mirror can be a subset, re-encoded, or a different alignment variant.

Each reference was checked with the Kaggle API rather than by opening the page,
which found two things:

- **`kpvisionlab/tufts-face-database` is not the dataset.** It holds one file of
  1551 bytes. Citing it would send someone after a stub expecting a face database,
  so Tufts keeps the request form at tdface.ece.tufts.edu.
- **The LFW copy is `lfw-deepfunneled`**, the deep-funneled alignment rather than
  raw LFW. Alignment variant moves verification accuracy, so this is the difference
  between reproducing the 6000-pair figures and quietly getting different ones. It
  was written down nowhere.

`curl` returns 404 for every Kaggle dataset URL, by the way. That is their bot
protection, not a dead link; the API disagreed with it on all four.

## Three dangling references, all predating this work

- `irlume_0.7.1_amd64.deb.asc`, a detached signature committed to the repo root by
  accident in an unrelated machine-API PR. The v0.7.1 release carries its own.
- `tpm.rs` pointed at `scripts/tpm-pcr-race-check.sh`; the file is `-swtpm.sh`.
- `fusion.rs` credited its Platt constants to `scripts/calibrate.py`, which has
  never existed in this repository. It now says the fit was done offline and that
  there is no such script, so nobody else goes looking.

## Checks

Packaging parity, action pins, the test-guard self-test (36/36) and `cargo check`
all pass after the moves. Every `scripts/*.sh|.py` path named anywhere in the tree
resolves. Both indexes verified in both directions: every file on disk appears in

items.body:
Continues from #13 (merged). Six commits. Everything below was measured or fetched, not assumed.

## The retirement was incomplete, and the docs were the worse half

Round 22 removed the 0-100 composite from the UI. It was still live in two other kinds of place:

- **README's headline benchmark table** carried a **Security** column printing `68 / 100` and
  `96 / 100`. A reader takes a README table as current results, and that pair is the worst artefact
  the metric produced: **16 of the 28 points separating them came from which arguments two call
  sites happened to supply**, not from cryptography. The column now reports the security *model*.
- **Six checklist rows** told a verifier to recompute the score. That is worse than stale, because a
  checklist is executed by a person - the row either wastes their time or produces a false failure
  against a panel that is behaving correctly.

Verified live after the fix: no `68 / 100`, no `96 / 100`, no legacy chart; results table reports
`security model`; the posture table renders.

### The parity trap this uncovered

The cross-implementation parity section held up the security score as its strongest example: Python
and TypeScript, written separately, both produced 68 and 96. They did - and the number was still
meaningless, because both faithfully reproduced the same argument-passing artefact.

**Agreement between two mirrors proves they match each other, not that either is right.** Every
parity check is now paired with an assertion against a source outside this repository.
`tests/test_decoy_reference.py` (Ma et al. PRA 72, 012326) and `npm run check:pqc` (NIST + C2SP
vectors) are the two that qualify, and the decoy model replaces the score as the example row.

## Confidentiality

The private business notes are confidential, so a public file listing their **filenames** has leaked
something even though the files are absent. Removed from `README.md`, `docker/env/Caddyfile` and
`docs/deliverable-verification.md`.

**Three references deliberately kept**: `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore` carry the patterns that keep
those files untracked, and the `Makefile` guard fails the build if one ever becomes tracked. Deleting
those would make the files committable - strictly worse than naming them in a build script.

## A dependency claim that flattered itself

*"node-seal is on SEAL 4.1.2, and that is upstream's newest."* Which upstream? True of node-seal,
false of Microsoft SEAL. Measured 2026-08-09: node-seal 7.0.0 **is** still newest on npm, but SEAL
has shipped **six releases** since 4.1.2 and reached **4.4.3 on 2026-08-04**. 4.4.0 is described only
as "Major security update"; 4.4.3 fixes null-pointer dereferences and C++ exceptions crossing the
**C API** boundary. Whether those reach an Emscripten/WASM build is now written as **unverified**.
No CVE, no GHSA - version history recorded as fact, no vulnerability claimed, gap noted as widening.

## The CKKS security notion nobody had written down

`IND-CPA-D` / `CPAD` appeared nowhere in any tracked doc, in a product that returns a decrypted
class. No false claim was made, so this is a gap. `docs/threat-model.md` now states: CKKS is IND-CPA,
not IND-CPA-D; ePrint 2026/203 (verified against the abstract page) proves an **impossibility** for
the HELLHO class - basic BFV, BGV, CKKS, TFHE - plus key recovery on DE-CKKS in OpenFHE in hours; the
browser demo is the benign case because the key holder is the person seeing the result; a server-side
deployment returning decrypted results would need noise flooding first.

## The nearest unmet compliance date

Art. 50(1) is implemented. **Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking of synthetic text is not**, and the
Agentic AI panel generates text. The AI Omnibus grace runs to **2 December 2026**. Recorded in the
roadmap with the design decision open.

items.title: docs: move the three root docs, add a guide, make the index a path
items.body:
`docs/` had a reference, a rationale, a roadmap, a gallery and a benchmark —
and nothing that taught the language. A reader's route was README's one example
straight into a 487-line reference, which says what a file *may contain* and
never what to write.

`docs/guide.md` is that missing page, and it is one page. Five ideas, in the
order they bite:

1. a dimension is declared, its coordinates usually are not;
2. absence is how you say sparse — `where` removes columns, it does not zero
   them;
3. a dimension can carry coordinates, and that is your topology;
4. `roll` and `shift` reach along an axis;
5. an equation's dims must equal its `foreach`.

Then `check`/`solve`, and — before any of it — **what the language will not
do**: bounds take a name or a number and never arithmetic (#31, which has bitten
a real port), and every expression is affine, which is the ceiling rather than
a gap.

Every expression it teaches is copied from a model in `examples/` that the
suite runs, and a test asserts that. A tutorial demonstrating syntax the
compiler no longer accepts is worse than no tutorial, and prose is exactly what
nothing else would notice drifting. The dimension blocks are deliberately
exempt: they are written compactly to be read rather than pasted.

`docs/README.md` leads with where to start instead of listing artifacts
alphabetically, and states which pages are generated — the construct matrix,
the benchmark tables, the chart numbers — so nobody hand-edits one.

440 passed / 1 xfailed, ruff and pyrefly clean.

Two commits: the move (pure renames — review with rename detection), then the guide and index.

**The move never reached `main`.** #259 merged into `docs/models-gallery` *after* that branch had squash-merged, so it landed on a dead branch. Re-applied here.

items.title: Correct adaptive pooling and zero-op counting rules
items.body:
## What

Correct the counting rules that can be fixed completely on the supported PyTorch range:

- Adaptive average pooling now sums the integer windows PyTorch actually pools instead of using a fractional input/output ratio.
- Nearest and nearest-exact upsampling count zero arithmetic operations; interpolation costs stay in the hook that owns them.
- GroupNorm and RMSNorm reuse the existing normalization rule.
- The README benchmark rows are refreshed for the nearest-upsampling correction.
- Bump the package patch version from 2.1.1 to 2.1.2 so this final PR triggers the release after the preceding fixes merge.

The proposed MultiheadAttention rule was removed during review. It crashed on valid keyword-only calls because PyTorch 1.8 forward hooks cannot observe keyword arguments, and profile_origin() does not hook composite modules. Shipping partial coverage or a compatibility branch would regress valid models rather than solve the problem.

## Validation

- 20 existing tests pass.
- Ruff and formatting checks pass.
- Exhaustive AdaptiveAvgPool1d/2d/3d checks across small input/output shapes match the exact PyTorch window boundaries.
- GroupNorm, RMSNorm, nearest upsampling, keyword-only MultiheadAttention non-regression, and the 2.1.2 version were checked directly.

## Deleted

The incomplete MultiheadAttention rule and registration, calculate_adaptive_avg(), calculate_upsample(), and the one-consumer upsampling cost constant.

## 🛠️ PR Summary

<sub>Made with ❤️ by [Ultralytics Actions](https://www.ultralytics.com/actions)</sub>

### 🌟 Summary

THOP 2.1.2 improves operation counting for normalization, adaptive pooling, and upsampling layers, with refreshed YOLO benchmark values. 🚀

### 📊 Key Changes

- Added FLOP/MAC counting support for `nn.GroupNorm`.
- Added optional support for `nn.RMSNorm` in PyTorch 2.4 and newer.
- Improved adaptive average pooling calculations to account for actual pooling windows and avoid fractional operation counts.
- Updated upsampling operation estimates:
  - Supports `nearest-exact`.
  - Uses explicit per-element costs for linear, bilinear, bicubic, and trilinear modes.
  - Warns and safely defaults to zero operations for unsupported modes.
- Removed obsolete adaptive pooling and upsampling helper functions.
- Bumped the package version from `2.1.1` to `2.1.2`.
- Updated English and Chinese README benchmark tables with minor corrected values.

### 🎯 Purpose & Impact

- 📈 Produces more accurate and consistent computational-cost estimates for modern PyTorch models.
- 🧩 Improves profiling coverage for models using GroupNorm and RMSNorm, including newer architectures.
- 🛠️ Makes upsampling estimates clearer and more maintainable across supported interpolation modes.
- ✅ Prevents fractional operation totals from adaptive average pooling calculations.
- 📚 Keeps published YOLOv8, YOLO11, and YOLO26 benchmark results aligned with the updated profiling behavior.

items.title: fix: reject spec-invalid directives, cap key-cache memory, show README benchmarks as ratios
items.body:
## What & why

Independent, low-risk fixes surfaced by a whole-repository code-review audit, bundled into one PR (to avoid repeated rebases against the in-flight `src/core.ts` PRs). The larger / design-dependent findings from the same audit are filed as their own issues (#126–#135, #138–#141).

**1. Reject two spec-invalid directives** — Closes #124, Closes #125.
- A **repeated `%TAG` for the same handle** used to be silently accepted (last-wins); it now errors, per [YAML 1.2.2 §6.8.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#682-tag-directives) (Example 6.17):
  ```yaml
  %TAG ! !foo
  %TAG ! !foo
  ---
  bar
  ```
- A **`%YAML` directive with a higher major version** (e.g. `%YAML 2.0`) used to parse silently; it's now rejected, per [YAML 1.2.2 §6.8.1](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#681-yaml-directives). A higher *minor* (`1.3`) and `%YAML 1.1`/`1.2` are unaffected.
- Both match `js-yaml`; the yaml-test-suite score is unchanged (364/373). Recorded in README's "Decisions and deviations" as intentional strictness over the lenient `yaml` library.

**2. Cap the key-intern cache to bound peak memory** — Closes #136.
- `keyCache` had no size limit (its sibling caches do), so an all-distinct-key document (e.g. a UUID/hostname/timestamp lookup table) grew it unbounded. It's now capped by **cumulative key size (4 MB default)**, and the cap is exposed as an opt-in `optimizations.keyCacheMaxKb` on `parse`/`parseAll`. Parsed output is byte-for-byte unchanged; the `./yaml`/`./js-yaml` compat shims are untouched.

**3. Show the README benchmark table as ratios** — Closes #137.
- The hero table's absolute ms/MB drift with the benchmark box (the old numbers were stale, but the apparent "regression" was a CI-runner baseline shift — `JSON.parse`'s own numbers moved the same way, not a lightning-yaml regression). It now shows **ratios to `JSON.parse`** — parse ~2.1×, peak-RSS ~1.4× for lightning-yaml — which don't swing with the machine, sourced from the newest [`benchmark-data`](https://github.com/jbsiddall/lightning-yaml/tree/benchmark-data) run (commit `4ca6140`, 2026-07-23) with a visible provenance line. The stale "3–5× faster" speed claim was corrected too.

## Correctness gate

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` · `pnpm test` (59/59)
- [x] `pnpm test:unit` (440/440, incl. new directive + key-cache tests) · `pnpm test:stringify` (218/218)
- [x] `pnpm test:suite` — **364/373 (97.6%), unchanged** · `pnpm test:compat` — unchanged
- [x] `pnpm bench:self` — no regression (the key-cache byte-counter is O(1)/key; directive checks are cold-path)

## Code review

- [x] `/code-review` passed — **all eight reviewers approved at commit `fe6999cb87da`**. Pushing new commits invalidates this: re-run `/code-review` and update the hash until all reviewers approve the new HEAD.

Deferred non-blocking notes (would reset the unanimous sign-off for cosmetic gain): the `parse`/`parseAll` per-call option apply/restore is duplicated (tracked in #141), and a `dumpKeyCache` comment still says "mirror" though the two caps now use different strategies — both can ride the #141 cleanup.

## Changeset

- [x] Two changesets, both **minor** for `lightning-yaml`: `reject-malformed-directives` (the two new directive errors) and `cap-key-cache-memory` (adds the public `keyCacheMaxKb` option). The README change is docs-only.

## Correctness note

The two directive changes are the only parse-behavior changes, both spec-backed:
- Duplicate `%TAG` per handle — [§6.8.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#682-tag-directives): "It is an error to specify more than one `TAG` directive for the same handle in the same document." (`js-yaml` throws; the `yaml` oracle accepts, but per CLAUDE.md the spec adjudicates over the oracle — recorded as a sanctioned strictness in README.)
- Higher-major `%YAML` — [§6.8.1](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#681-yaml-directives): a higher major version "should be rejected with an appropriate error message." Only `major ≠ 1` is rejected.

The key-cache cap and README rework change no parse/dump behavior.

items.title: Performance improvements and guide update
items.body:
## Summary

Revamps the performance/benchmark suite, lands two structural performance improvements to the core locking paths (parallel multi-node I/O and configurable exponential backoff with jitter), brings the documentation back in line with the current API, and streamlines CI. Core code changes are additive and non-breaking.

## Core performance
- **Parallel multi-node I/O** (`MultiNodeStrategy`): acquire/release/extend now fan out per-node Redis operations concurrently via `CompletableFuture` on a shared daemon thread pool, waiting for the quorum on join. Per-attempt cost drops from  ~`N×RTT` to ~`max(RTT)` on multi-node clusters.
- **Exponential backoff with jitter**: new `BackoffCalculator` (`delay = min(maxRetryDelay, retryDelay × multiplier^attempt)`, optional jitter), applied in `PollingWaitStrategy`, the `Redlock` retry-loop fallback, and `RedlockReadWriteLock`. Replaces the fixed retry delay that caused contention storms. `FairLock` intentionally stays on tight polling.
- **Config**: `RedlockConfiguration` adds `maxRetryDelay`, `retryDelayMultiplier` (≥ 1.0), and `retryDelayJitterRatio` ([0.0, 1.0]), validated. Defaults preserve prior behavior (multiplier 1.0, jitter 0.0).
- **`LockWaitStrategy`**: attempt-aware `waitForRelease(key, timeout, attempt)` and a backoff-parameterized `initialize(...)` overload (both default-provided).

## Benchmarks & tests
- New `JsonReportGenerator` emits machine-readable JSON alongside markdown; per- primitive `*-benchmark-results.json` added; scenarios/clients and aggregation refactored; new `benchmark-analysis.md` with methodology and cross-library standings.
- Added `BackoffCalculatorTest`, `PollingWaitStrategyTest`, and new `RedlockConfigurationTest` cases.

## Documentation
- Full accuracy pass against the current API. Rewrote the getting-started path (`index`, `quick-start`, `basic-usage`, `redis-clients`, `best-practices`) off the removed legacy `new Redlock(pool…)` / `redlock.lock(key, ttl)` API to the
  `RedlockManager` factory (`withJedis`/`withLettuce` → `createLock`, JDK `Lock`, try-with-resources on the manager).
- API reference: fixed RxRedlock method names/return types, documented the new backoff config options and `database` node option.
- Architecture: corrected native CAS/CAD to Redis 8.4+, clarified polling uses the configurable `retryDelay` (default 200ms); regenerated stale benchmark tables to match the current results.
- Comparison docs: switched to factory usage, corrected `CountDownLatch.countDown` to atomic (`decrAndPublishIfZero`), fixed signatures, removed leftover fragments.
- Removed decorative emoji across the docs.

## CI
- `ci.yml`: consolidated unit + integration test steps, moved performance tests to `-Dgroups=performance`, and removed redundant report/code-quality/build-info jobs.
- Removed the standalone `pr-validation.yml` workflow.
- `nightly.yml`: dropped a redundant unit-test step.
- Added a Codecov coverage badge to the README.

## Compatibility
No breaking API changes. New config options are additive; new interface methods have defaults. Behavior is unchanged unless backoff is explicitly configured.

items.title: fix: evaluate in eval mode — BatchNorm in train mode corrupted every reported score
items.body:
## The bug

`_eval_test` in `run_standard_validation.py` is the **single path that produces every number this project publishes** — the benchmark table, the quick smoke, and the Kaggle runner all call this one function. It wrapped its forwards in `torch.no_grad()` but never called `net.eval()`. Those are not the same thing.

The spatial and volumetric schemas carry `BatchNorm` (the `norm` primitive, and the stems). Left in **train mode**, BatchNorm normalises each eval minibatch by *that minibatch's own* statistics instead of the running averages — so a reported score depends on how the test split happens to be ordered and batched. A train-mode forward also **updates the running buffers even under `no_grad`** (the update is a buffer write, not an autograd op), so merely evaluating leaked test statistics into the model.

`AllGraph._forward_new` (behind `predict`/`load`) has always called `net.eval()`. The runner and `predict` therefore disagreed about the same weights, which is what exposed this.

## Ranking metrics were hit ~100× harder than pointwise ones

ROC-AUC ranks logits across the **entire** test set, and per-batch normalisation puts logits from different batches on different scales — destroying cross-batch comparability. Accuracy is a per-sample argmax and barely notices.

Regenerating the two affected contracts (`--contracts spatial,volumetric`, published command otherwise unchanged):

| dataset | metric | published | corrected | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SynapseMNIST3D** | ROC-AUC | 0.5083 | **0.7573** | **+0.2490** |
| **VesselMNIST3D** | ROC-AUC | 0.6781 | **0.8990** | **+0.2210** |
| DiffusionBlob3D | R² | 0.9700 | 0.9892 | +0.0192 |
| OrganMNIST3D | acc | 0.9279 | 0.9361 | +0.0082 |
| MNISTAngle | R² | 0.7875 | 0.7909 | +0.0034 |
| MNIST | acc | 0.9918 | 0.9917 | −0.0001 |
| BloodMNIST | acc | 0.9421 | 0.9068 | −0.0354 |

The remaining **26 rows are byte-identical** — no other schema uses BatchNorm.

## The delta is measurement, not run variance

Scoring **one** new checkpoint both ways on the same data reproduces the old published values to four decimal places:

```
SynapseMNIST3D   ROC-AUC   eval-mode 0.7573   train-mode 0.5083   delta +0.2490
VesselMNIST3D    ROC-AUC   eval-mode 0.8990   train-mode 0.6781   delta +0.2210
```

Same weights, same data — so the retraining landed on equivalent models and the entire difference was how they were scored.

## What this changes substantively

**SynapseMNIST3D's published 0.5083 was indistinguishable from chance** and read as "the schema learns nothing on this dataset". It is actually **0.7573** against a ~0.82 literature reference — short of SOTA, but not a failure. VesselMNIST3D moves from clearly-behind to competitive (0.8990 vs ~0.87/~0.93).

The correction is **not uniformly favourable**: BloodMNIST drops to 0.9068 and now sits *below* its ~0.958 reference rather than above it. Direction isn't systematic, as expected when per-batch statistics are sometimes a better and sometimes a worse fit than the running averages.

Also fixes the same defect in `run_cellpainting_validation`'s two eval paths, which route to the spatial schema and were affected identically (retrieval mAP and accuracy).

## Regression tests

`tests_unit/test_eval_test_mode.py` pins the invariants from the outside: a score must be invariant to test-split permutation and to eval batch size, evaluating must not mutate the model, and the runner must agree with `predict()` on the same weights. Verified they genuinely fail without the fix — 0.4609 vs 0.8750 order-dependence, and 9 mutated BatchNorm buffers including `stem.1.running_mean`.

## Bring-your-own-dataset results (Kaggle)

New README section, **generated** by `make_results_table --kaggle` from the Kaggle runner's separate results document into its own marker region (the two regions cannot collide — a test asserts each marker appears exactly once). First three datasets, all fitted under the benchmark suite's exact pipeline flags:

| dataset | acc | chance | skill | architecture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BloodCells | 0.8010 | 0.2509 | +0.7343 | `conv_dw→pointwise→atrous` |
| BrainTumorMRI | 0.7887 | 0.2500 | +0.7183 | `conv_dw→pointwise→norm` |
| ChestXrayPneumonia | 0.8798 | 0.6250 | +0.6795 | `pointwise→pointwise→norm→conv_dw` |

ChestXrayPneumonia is why the table reports `skill`: its chance baseline is **0.6250** (3:1 class skew), so its highest-in-table accuracy is its lowest-in-table skill. Verified it isn't degenerate — NORMAL recall 0.821, PNEUMONIA 0.915.

The renderer distinguishes **three** epoch states rather than two: `converged` is `None` when no `--auto_epoch` criterion ran, and reusing the benchmark table's `†` ("stopped at the ceiling without converging") would assert something that was never measured.

`run_kaggle_validation` now records the invoking command on each row — `meta.runs` accumulates across invocations and can't be attributed back to a specific row, so an ad-hoc dataset's row otherwise couldn't say how it was produced.

## Verification

- `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` clean (162 files)

items.title: feat(bench): add succinct library comparison benchmarks and ADR-0011
items.body:
## Description

This PR addresses issue #47 by adding comprehensive benchmarking and documentation for succinctly's rank/select implementation against other maintained Rust succinct-structure crates (vers-vecs, sucds, and sux). The work includes both empirical measurements and an Architecture Decision Record (ADR-0011) that records the build-vs-buy reasoning behind implementing custom succinct structures in-crate rather than depending on existing libraries.

Prior to this PR, the repository could not answer whether existing crates were evaluated or benchmarked. The documentation incorrectly claimed ~3% space overhead for the rank directory (the Poppy paper's figure, not this implementation's). This PR corrects the record with measured data and honest assessment of trade-offs.

## Type of Change
- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) — `succinct_libs` benchmark suite
- [x] Documentation update — ADR-0011, benchmark page, corrected space overhead claims
- [x] Test coverage improvement — comparison verification in benchmark

## Related Issue
Fixes #47 — "Evaluate existing succinct crates and benchmark against them"

## Changes Made

**Benchmark Implementation:**
- Added `bench-compare/benches/succinct_libs.rs` with comprehensive rank/select comparison across four libraries
- Implemented `TrackingAllocator` for precise resident-size measurement
- Created `verify_agreement` test ensuring all four libraries agree on rank1/select1 answers before timing
- Benchmarks test construction, rank1 (10,000 random queries), select1, and resident memory across 1M-10M bits at 10/50/90% density
- Added `succinct_libs` benchmark to registry in `src/bin/succinctly/bench_runner/registry.rs`
- Updated `bench-compare/Cargo.toml` with dependencies: `vers-vecs`, `sucds`, `sux`, `rand`, `rand_chacha` (all pinned for reproducibility)
- Updated `bench-compare/Cargo.toml` to enable `simd` feature for succinctly and vers-vecs

**Documentation:**
- Created `docs/adrs/adr-0011.md` — Architecture Decision Record documenting why succinct structures are built in-crate
  - Records three requirements: `no_std` support (no existing crate satisfies), balanced-parentheses tree navigation (none provide), hinted select (none expose)
  - Honestly reports that BitVec wins no measured category on ARM64: sux is 1.5-1.7x faster at rank/select, vers-vecs is 5-8x more compact and faster to build
  - Documents why BitVec is kept despite losing: only `no_std` requirement currently holds; BalancedParens and JsonIndex bypass BitVec entirely
  - Lists alternatives evaluated and rejected (vers-vecs, sux, sucds, succinct, fid, bio) with rationale
- Created `docs/benchmarks/rust-succinct-libs.md` — benchmark results and methodology
  - Platforms: ARM64 only (Apple M5 Max); flags x86_64 run as outstanding
  - Resident size table: vers-vecs 5-8x more compact; succinctly 27.5-47.5% overhead rising with density
  - Construction: vers-vecs 1.0-1.31x faster
  - rank1: succinctly 1.8-2.3x faster than vers-vecs, but sux 1.5-1.7x faster than succinctly
  - select1: sux 3-4x faster; marked as noisy (~40% variance in individual cells)
  - Documents fairness caveat: sucds/sux lack bulk-word constructor, must fill per-bit
- Updated `docs/adrs/README.md` to add ADR-0011 entry
- Updated `docs/architecture/README.md` — noted Prior Art now includes Rust crates evaluated
- Corrected `docs/architecture/bitvec.md` — rank directory overhead documented as ~25% (128 bits per 512 bits), not ~3%; full BitVec 27.5-47.5% resident
- Comprehensively updated `docs/architecture/prior-art.md`
  - Clarified Poppy paper claims 3% but succinctly's directory costs ~25% by design
  - Added table of Rust succinct libraries with versions, `no_std` status, and assessments
  - Documented sucds `no_std` attribute is vestigial in 0.8.3 — builds fail with ~141 errors
  - Cross-referenced ADR-0011 and benchmark page
- Updated `docs/benchmarks/README.md` — added rust-succinct-libs row to benchmark table
- Updated `docs/benchmarks/inventory.md` — added rust-succinct-libs.md (4 sections)
- Updated `docs/log.md` with 2026-07-15 entry documenting sources ingested and corrections made
- Updated `docs/optimizations/cache-memory.md` — rank directory overhead corrected from 3% to ~25%
- Updated `docs/optimizations/hierarchical-structures.md` — rank/select overhead corrected to reflect actual measurements
- Updated `CLAUDE.md` — BitVec performance summary corrected from ~3-4% to ~28-48% overhead
- Updated `README.md` — corrected feature claims from "~3% space overhead" to "tuned for query speed over compactness (~28-48% overhead)"
- Updated README core structures documentation with link to benchmark results

## Testing

**Automated Testing:**
- [x] All existing tests pass
- [x] New benchmark suite added with verification step (`verify_agreement` ensures all four libraries agree on rank1/select1 answers)
- [x] Benchmark registered and accessible via `bench run succinct_libs` command

**Manual Testing:**
- [x] Benchmarks tested on ARM64 (Apple M5 Max)
- [x] `cargo test` passes with all benchmarks
- [x] `cargo clippy` clean
- [x] `cargo fmt` applied

### Test Commands
```bash
# Run the new benchmark suite
cd bench-compare
cargo bench --bench succinct_libs

# Or via the bench runner
succinctly bench run succinct_libs

# Verify all tests pass
cargo test --all

# Check code quality
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
```

## Performance Impact
- [x] No performance impact to main crate (benchmarks are in `bench-compare` standalone crate)
- Benchmark findings documented: succinctly's BitVec trades space for query speed; loses on space (vers-vecs 5-8x better), loses on select (sux 3-4x faster), competitive on rank, faster to build than sux/sucds

## Checklist
- [x] My code follows the project's style guidelines
- [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code
- [x] I have added comprehensive documentation explaining the decision
- [x] Benchmark code includes verification logic (`verify_agreement`)
- [x] New and existing tests pass locally
- [x] Documentation is complete and accurate (corrected prior misstated overhead figures)
- [x] No new warnings generated

## Additional Notes

**Honest Assessment**: This PR deliberately reports findings as they came out rather than as a defense of the existing code. The measurements show BitVec loses on space and select performance but wins on rank speed (among the measured libraries). The decision to keep it in-crate is justified by three requirements: `no_std` (which no external crate satisfies), balanced-parentheses tree navigation, and hinted select — only the first currently applies to BitVec itself. The code acknowledges that BalancedParens and JsonIndex bypass BitVec entirely, making its use a candidate for replacement (tracked in issue #228).

**Platform Limitations**: Results are ARM64-only (Apple M5 Max). Succinctly's x86_64 popcount is AVX-512 VPOPCNTDQ-gated and untested here. Vers-vecs' SIMD select is also AVX-512-gated, so an x86_64 run could change the placings and is flagged as outstanding. The resident-size measurements are deterministic and platform-independent.

**Space Overhead Corrections**: Four documents claimed ~3% overhead for the rank directory. That is the Poppy paper's figure, not succinctly's implementation. All instances have been corrected to the measured value: ~25% for the rank directory alone, 27.5-47.5% for the full BitVec with select index (rising with density). This was an arithmetic error in bitvec.md that propagated through the docs.

**Future Work**: ADR-0011 recommends revisiting this decision if the `no_std` requirement is dropped or if sucds fixes its `no_std` build. The benchmark provides a stable baseline for that future evaluation.

items.title: fix(docs): correct seven stale component counts, guard the class in CI
items.body:
## What

Fixes seven stale component counts that are shipping right now, then makes the class mechanically impossible to reintroduce.

| # | File:line | Said | Should be |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `AGENTS.md:33` | 11 reusable agent templates | 12 |
| 2 | `AGENTS.md:34` | 18 reusable skill templates | 19 |
| 3 | `README.md:97` | "We give you **11**" | 12 |
| 4 | `i18n/README.ja.md:107` | `**11個**` | 12 |
| 5 | `i18n/README.ko.md:107` | `**11개**` | 12 |
| 6 | `i18n/README.zh.md:107` | `**11 个**` | 12 |
| 7 | `docs/SETTINGS-GUIDE.md:292` | 8 lifecycle events | 9 |

Rows 3 to 6 are one bug replicated in four languages. That is the case worth automating: a contributor who fixes the English line has three translated copies to remember, in scripts they may not read.

`AGENTS.md` is the first file an AI assistant reads to orient itself in the repo, so a wrong count there is wrong at the point of maximum leverage.

## Why a CI guard, and why now

Stale counts have been corrected four separate times in this release cycle: the visual assets, `setup.sh`, the "43 automated tests" figure, and now these seven. Each fix was a manual sweep, and each missed some. `tests/count-check.sh` derives every expected value from the filesystem and asserts that each published copy agrees.

Adding a thirteenth agent now fails **17 bindings across 13 files** and names every one, which is the checklist a contributor previously had to reconstruct by hand.

## Why a registry rather than a prose sweep

The obvious design is to scan prose for `<digit> <category>` and compare. I built that first and measured it. It produced **7 false positives and missed 4 real bugs**:

- **False positives**, all legitimate text: per-preset deltas (`Add 4 hooks + 2 agents`), adoption rows (`CLAUDE.md + 2 hooks`), and card markup where three whole cards share one line so "the number nearest the label" is a coin flip.
- **Misses**, all real: `11 reusable agent templates` (an adjective splits the digit from the category), a bare `**11**` whose category is in the previous clause, and the three CJK counter forms where the category sits in another clause and another script.

`SETUP.md` settles the question: `+ 4 more hooks, 2 agents` and `+ all 12 agents, 19 skills` sit one line apart in the same table. Totals and deltas are not lexically separable, so no amount of regex tuning fixes the sweep.

So the guard registers what is right instead of excluding what is wrong: an explicit `(file, anchor, expected)` binding per published total, with every expected value derived from the filesystem.

**Trade-off, stated plainly:** a registry cannot catch a count introduced in a brand-new location tomorrow, which a sweep theoretically could. But the sweep's measured behavior was 11 wrong verdicts out of 13, so its theoretical reach bought nothing. When you add a new published count, add a binding. A `MISSING_ANCHOR` failure is how the guard tells you a document was reworded out from under it, rather than silently checking nothing.

**Bindings are per-line, not per-file, because a file is not a trust boundary.** `i18n/README.ko.md` states our agent count on line 107 and Project-AI-MemoryCore's "11 feature extensions" on line 303, in the same CJK counter form. A file-level rule would either miss the bug or corrupt a third-party credit. Anchors bind to surrounding text, so they cannot drift onto the wrong line.

## CI wiring

Only the `push` trigger is widened (to include `**/*.md` and `assets/**`). The `pull_request` trigger deliberately keeps **no path filter**, per the existing comment: a required check that is skipped on some PRs would block their merge forever.

## Verification

- Guard run on the **unfixed** tree: failed with exactly the 7 findings above and no false positives. A guard that passes on a known-broken tree is measuring nothing.
- Guard after the fixes: **56 pass / 0 fail**.
- Adversarial: added a 13th agent (17 bindings fail across 13 files), a 20th skill, a 7th rule, and a 22nd battle story; each was caught and each reverted cleanly to green.
- False-positive pass: preset deltas, adoption rows, `up to 4 agents`, Cursor's `~11 hook types`, the benchmark tables, `minimal 3-file setup`, and the 4/10/20/55 preset file counts are all untouched and unflagged.
- `hooks/test-hooks.sh`: still exactly **55 pass / 0 fail**, proving the guard did not inflate the very number it asserts.
- `tests/install-matrix.sh`: **19 passed / 0 failed**.
- Portability: passes under `LC_ALL=C` (the CJK anchors are locale-independent) and when invoked from an arbitrary working directory. No `python`, `jq`, or `node` dependency in executed code. LF line endings, enforced by the existing `.gitattributes`.

Two rounds of adversarial review were run against the guard itself, and both found real defects that are fixed here: unbound battle-story counts and an unbound `docs/WHY.md` tier line (dead ground truth that shipped the appearance of a check), a card matcher that silently skipped `assets/card-social-preview.html` entirely, a sum check that accepted `14 + 1 = 15` while both addends were wrong, and a missing ambiguity guard in `card()` that made a duplicated label resolve by document order.

## What

Fixes the **"red veil"** rendering bug and refreshes the benchmark at the corrected prompt.

### The bug
The scene-extraction prompt left `backdrop.color` with **no neutral default**. On a request that named no backdrop, the LLM invented a color (often **red**), which — with a gray world and white lights — bled a colored cast over otherwise-neutral packshots.

### The fix
- `product_render_extractor.py`: honor **any named backdrop shade** (including gray nuances `cool_gray` / `warm_gray` / `neutral_gray`); fall back to `neutral_gray` **only** when no backdrop is described.
- `index.html`: Console presets now name their backdrop explicitly.

A first, over-aggressive wording regressed `v0-sphere` ("fond gris froid" → overridden to neutral_gray); the shipped version fixes that — verified on the benchmark.

items.title: Lead the README with a visual comparison, fix the node counter, name the prior art
items.body:
## What this changes

Three things, in the order they happened.

**A comparison figure at the top of the README.** The README opened with two benchmark tables, which is the wrong first ten seconds for someone arriving from a link. The interesting claim is about geometry, so the figure shows geometry: four cases × input, Open Vectorizer, VTracer, potrace, with a marker on every on-curve node each engine emitted. It is generated by a new `figure` binary in `benchmarks/shootout` from the same case directory as the tables, not drawn by hand. The `blob` row is included deliberately — it is the case where potrace beats us.

**A real bug in the shootout's node counter.** Building the figure meant extracting node positions, which exposed it. The counter counted drawing *segments*, but generators disagree about how to close a shape: potrace ends its last curve on the starting point and writes `z`, we write `Z` and let it draw the closing edge. Segment counting therefore charged potrace for a node it does not have and let us off one we do — understating our own counts by one per closed subpath. It was already visible in the README, where the same rotated square cost 4 nodes in the ground-truth table and 3 in the shootout table.

The parser now collects the actual on-curve points of each subpath and drops a final point that merely repeats the start, so both conventions agree. It moved to `shootout::nodes` and is shared with the figure, so the dots in the picture and the numbers under it cannot drift apart. It has unit tests covering both closing conventions, implicit command repetition, relative commands and holes.

**Naming the prior art.** A benchmark listing only the engines it beats invites the obvious question. Vectorizer.AI is the closest thing to this approach that exists — its feature list describes placing boundaries from anti-aliasing pixel values and fitting parameterized circles, ellipses, rounded rectangles and stars, which is further than we go. It is commercial, closed, and has no published method, so it cannot be benchmarked, but it should be named by us rather than by the first person to notice. Also credited: the partial-area-effect literature for locating an edge from the area it covers in a pixel, and Yang et al. 2023 for applying that to clip-art vectorization with a learned model. The claim left standing is the open, deterministic, measurable version, which is narrower and true.

## Benchmark

The engine is untouched — this is the harness, the docs and one image, so the synthetic benchmark is unchanged and irrelevant to the diff. The evidence that matters is the shootout, rerun in full against potrace 1.16, VTracer 0.6.5 and `rsvg-convert` for scoring.

Every accuracy and area figure reproduced exactly. Node counts changed only where the counter was wrong:

| case | ours before | ours after | potrace | vtracer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| rotated square | 3 | **4** | 5 | 49 |
| triangle | 2 | **3** | 7 | 40 |
| 5-point star | 9 | **10** | 20 | 76 |
| thick L | 5 | **6** | 12 | 10 |
| square (on white) | 7 | **9** | – | 8 |
| wordmark (on white) | 20 | **24** | – | 23 |
| three-colour mark (on white) | 70 | **81** | – | 183 |

Ours go up; potrace and VTracer are unchanged, because both close their paths explicitly. Both README tables are updated throughout. The timing column is left alone — it was measured on the author's machine and node counts are machine-independent.

The corrected numbers cost us four cases on node count in Table 2. All but one are the same effect rather than better geometry: on opaque input we emit the background as a shape with the artwork punched out of it, so every contour is paid for twice — 7 of the 9 nodes on `square`. That is now stated in the README and tracked in `TODO.md` as a contribution, along with the caveat that dropping the hole depends on what partly transparent artwork needs.

The remaining loss is honest: on `blob`, the one shape with no primitive and no corners to exploit, potrace's curve fitting is a node ahead of ours. It is in the figure for that reason.

## Checks

- [x] `cargo test --workspace` passes
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes, and the shootout's own workspace too
- [x] Output is still deterministic — no engine code changed, and regenerating the figure after the clippy fix produced a byte-identical SVG
- [x] New behaviour has a test — five unit tests on the node parser in `benchmarks/shootout/src/nodes.rs`
- [x] No new dependency

## Anything else

The figure excludes the background rectangle each engine emits on an opaque input. Leaving it in scattered markers around the border of half the panels and told the reader nothing; the rule is applied to every engine identically, and it is stated in the caption and in `benchmarks/README.md`, where the tables still count the whole file. If you would rather the figure and the tables agree exactly at the cost of the noise, that is a reasonable call and an easy change.

Two smaller judgement calls worth a second opinion. The committed PNG is 94KB, rendered at 2× and put through `pngquant`; the command is documented in `benchmarks/README.md` so it can be rebuilt, but it is the first binary in a repo that has deliberately kept fixtures in memory. And a recovered primitive is one node, so its marker sits at the centre of the circle rather than on the outline — explained in the caption, but it does read oddly for a second.

A brightgreen `338/338 (100%)` badge sat at the top, repeated three more times.

**338 is the size of the CIS RHEL 9 benchmark** — true, and kept as the why-not-build-your-own argument. It is **not** our measured coverage. The modules reference **224 distinct CIS control IDs**.

Milestone 2 of `.claude/prds/ranking-benchmark.prd.md`. `benchmarks/score.py` turns the baseline I measured by hand in Milestone 1 into something a contributor runs before opening a PR.

**No ranking behavior changed.**

```
$ python benchmarks/score.py

| Target | Candidates | Labels | Rank of each label | recall@10 | Median rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| click 8.4.2 | 152 | 4 | 1, 2, 38, 39 | 2/4 | 20 |
| pluggy 1.6.0 | 20 | 3 | 5, 6, 14 | 2/3 | 6 |
| sqlalchemy 2.0.51 | 2092 | 5 | 620, 1287, 1369, 1628, 1631 | 0/5 | 1369 |

Aggregate recall@10: 4/12
```

## The acceptance test earned its keep

The script had to reproduce the table committed to `benchmarks/README.md` **before the script existed**. It disagreed in one cell — click's median rank — and the script was right: `median({1,2,38,39}) = 20`, not the `20.5` the README recorded from a by-hand slip. Fixed the README to match the tool, not the other way round.

## Design

- **Script in `benchmarks/`, not a CLI subcommand.** The PRD scopes this as internal instrumentation with no user-facing feature. `modscan benchmark` would be surface maintained for nobody.
- **Not a `tests/test_*.py` file.** CI globs that pattern and scoring needs the three targets installed — it'd fail or skip in CI for no signal. The metric maths is factored into pure functions covered by `tests/test_benchmark_scoring.py`, which stays offline and CI-safe.
- **Version mismatch skips with a notice, never a misleading score.**
- **A label the detector never surfaces counts at `candidates+1`, not dropped** — dropping would let a change that loses a seam entirely *improve* the median.

items.title: fix(ci): store the anon key as a secret, not a repo variable
items.body:
## Correcting a bad call from #338

I stored `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` as a repo **variable**, reasoning it was "public by design — it ships in the browser bundle." I checked that claim instead of assuming it, and it's false.

I scanned every JS chunk served from production: **the key is in none of them.** The training-facility routes that would inline it are flag-gated off in prod — `/training-facility/gym/otf` returns 404 there. So the anon key has no public consumer today.

That matters because RLS is `using (true)` for reads on the cardio, OTF, and benchmark tables. Right now that key is the only thing between the internet and the fitness data.

And this repo is public, which makes its **Actions logs public**. GitHub redacts secrets from logs; variables it prints verbatim. Storing an unpublished credential as a variable traded real protection for a tidier-looking reference.

## Changes

- Moved the key to a repo secret; deleted the variable (both already done on the repo).
- Workflow now reads `secrets.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`.
- Corrected the wrong rationale everywhere it had propagated: the workflow comment, the script, `scripts/README.md`, and both RPC migration comments. **Comment-only in the `.sql` files** — the applied DDL is unchanged, so the ledger still matches and `migrations:check` stays green.

## What this does and doesn't buy

Worth being precise, because it's easy to overclaim: masking stops **accidental** logging, not a malicious PR — that can print anything in its env either way. What actually protects this job is that nothing privileged is in it, which was the point of the service-role swap in #338.

The distinction that carries the weight: service-role **bypasses RLS and can write**; the anon key is **read-only and policy-bounded**. Swapping those was the security fix. Secret-vs-variable is the smaller, cheap improvement on top.

## Note

The key was printed in my session transcript via `gh variable list` before this change. If you'd rather not rely on that being private, rotating the publishable key in the Supabase dashboard is quick and I can update the secret after.

## Verification

- Drift check runs green against production with the anon key
- 8 drift unit tests pass; eslint clean
- Grep confirms no remaining "public by design / ships in the bundle" claims (the one surviving "public by construction" refers to *migration names*, which is accurate — they're on GitHub)
